title: Suhayb the Roman
hook: who gave all his wealth to be allowed to emigrate, and was told, the trade was profitable (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ka'b ibn Malik, who had no excuse and said so. Your line was: truth saved him. What small truth did you tell that cost you something? Day eight hundred fifty-three.

The road out of Mecca is blocked. A man is trying to leave for Medina, where the Prophet and his companions have gone, and some men of Quraysh stand in his way. They have a point to make, and it's about money. You came here with nothing, they tell him. You got rich among us. And now you want to walk off with all of it? Not a chance. He could argue. He could fight. He could turn back and wait for a better day. Instead he asks them a question. Today: Suhayb, called the Roman.
screen: `THE ROAD OUT IS BLOCKED.` → `YOU GOT RICH AMONG US.` → `HE ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the early biographies of the Prophet. Suhayb's question to the men on the road was simple. If I give you my wealth, will you let me go? They said yes. So he told them where it was, handed it over, and left for Medina with nothing. When word of it reached the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he said, as the biographies tell it: Suhayb has profited. Suhayb has profited. Why the Roman? Tradition says Suhayb was an Arab by birth who was carried off as a child and grew up among the Byzantines, the Romans of that time, until his speech carried their accent, and later came to Mecca, where he made his living as a trader. So he knew exactly what money was, and what a deal was. That's what makes the Prophet's words land. He didn't say Suhayb was generous, or brave. He spoke a trader's language back to a trader. You've made a profit. Some commentators on the Qur'an connect Suhayb to a verse in surah two about a person who sells his own self, seeking the good pleasure of God. Not every commentator links the verse to him, and the verse speaks for itself either way. But the picture is the same. Everything on one side of the scale. On the other, the road to where he wanted to be. A roadblock like that may never come. The question can still come in small sizes. What would you give up, to go where you want to go? A comfort, a habit, an evening. The trade the Prophet praised was not a loss dressed up as virtue. He called it a profit.
screen: `IF I GIVE YOU MY WEALTH, WILL YOU LET ME GO?` · `SUHAYB HAS PROFITED.` · `A TRADER'S WORD TO A TRADER.` · `ONE WHO SELLS HIS OWN SELF.` · then, large: `A PROFITABLE TRADE.`

segments.voice: The practice: trade a comfort for a good. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small comfort that's been standing between you and something good. An extra hour of scrolling that could be a call to your mother. A takeout order that could be a gift to someone who needs it. A lie-in that could be a dawn prayer, if you pray, or a walk. Breathe in, and hold both sides of the trade. Breathe out, and choose one. Don't make it big. Make it real. The bell holds the time.
Suhayb. The trader who handed over his wealth to be let go to Medina, and was told by the Prophet that he had profited. Today's word.
Your line: a profitable trade. Today, make the trade you chose, one comfort given up for one good done. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims tell Suhayb's story from the early biographies of the Prophet, and some commentators read it alongside surah 2:207, about one who sells himself seeking God's pleasure.

original.note: Arabic: Suhayb al-Rumi, Suhayb the Roman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who lost everything to get away.
what it means: a trader who traded his wealth for the road to Medina, and was told he had made a profit.
what a scholar hears: the Prophet's verb is a merchant's word for gain; in some versions it is the sale that has profited. some commentators connect the story to surah 2:207.
